newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui army dissidents hand in more heavy weapons.
newsitem.headline: Bangui army dissidents hand in more heavy weapons.

text.p: Army dissidents in the Central African Republic capital Bangui handed in more heavy weapons on Tuesday as part of a four-day truce that ended a week of bloody clashes with African peacekeepers, witnesses said.

A spokesman for the peacekeepers, who deployed in Bangui under a January 25 peace deal to end three army mutinies in under a year, said that before Tuesday's handovers the dissidents had turned in 13 of their 40 mortars.
The truce between army dissidents, among a minority who had yet to rejoin their units under the January deal, and the peacekeepers runs until 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday evening.

Under the truce, negotiated by Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure, architect of the January deal, the army dissidents hand their mortars over to France's ambassador in the city.
Another aim was to give families of the 100 or so people killed in the clashes, many of them civilians, time to bury their dead.
Elsewhere in the battered city, shops, offices, banks and markets were open despite an underlying uncertainty on what would happen next.
Some of the 60,000 civilians who fled the Central African Republic capital in fear of their lives trickled back home on Monday as the truce held, relief workers said.
The clashes began on June 20 after an incident between peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers.
President Ange-Felix Patasse, the mutineers and representatives of all political groups and society at large signed the January deal.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
Former colonial power France has troops in the country under a defence pact. It intervened to restore order in January and then handed over to the peacekeepers.
Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo have troops in the 800-strong force. Patasse opponents criticise the Chadians, saying Patasse hired Chadians in a private militia.
